# Appendix: Supported Senses

<!-- Generated by 'WordSense.Builder appendix' from data and corpus/anchors. Do not edit. -->

## How Answers Work

WordSense identifies the sense of a word in its sentence. The inventory of senses is the one of Open English WordNet for
the lemmas of one word, plus a few project senses for the words that Open English WordNet does not cover (for example
`the#determiner`). The lemma is the dictionary form of the word (for example `record`); a word such as `records` is
matched to its lemma through the forms listed below. An answer is a lemma, a part of speech and, where the model is
trained for the lemma, a sense or a group of senses.

### Senses

Every sense has a readable id of the form `lemma#label` (for example `bank#coin-bank`) that is stable and never reused
for another meaning, and is linked to one Open English WordNet sense key. A project sense has no key. The senses of a
lemma and part of speech are listed most frequent first, by the WordNet 3.0 tag count of the sense key; a project sense
ranks last. Each sense is listed with its gloss, the definition of its Open English WordNet synset.

### Parts of Speech

The `PartOfSpeech` enumeration defines ten parts of speech: the eight classic ones, `Determiner` and `Auxiliary`. The
trained lemmas listed here, which give the context answers, have senses of 7 of them. A dictionary answer can also be a
part of speech of a lemma that is not listed, as the answer for a word with one part of speech or as a candidate of a
word that has several. The table counts the trained lemmas and senses of each part of speech:

| Part of speech | Lemmas | Senses |
| -------------- | -----: | -----: |
| `Noun`         |     13 |     69 |
| `Verb`         |     14 |     80 |
| `Adjective`    |     15 |     72 |
| `Adverb`       |     15 |     72 |
| `Conjunction`  |      1 |      1 |
| `Interjection` |      3 |      3 |
| `Determiner`   |      2 |      2 |

### Groups

A **group** is optional. It exists only where it was curated: a set of at least two, but not all, senses of one lemma
and part of speech that are closely related in meaning and that a reader can confuse. A sense is in at most one group
and needs none; the sense lines below show `none` for a sense in no group. When the model cannot tell the senses of a
group apart it answers with the group, which is the level between the part of speech and the sense.

### Pronunciations

A sense has a **respelling**, a short plain spelling of its pronunciation, only when its pronunciation differs from the
other senses of its lemma, for example the noun and the verb of a heteronym. The library has no phonetic data of its
own; a consumer such as a speech synthesizer keeps its own pronunciations keyed by sense id. A sense without a
respelling shows none below, and a group never mixes two respellings.

### Forms

Inflected forms are mapped to their lemma by the forms of the word table, so `presents` is analyzed as a form of
`present`. Each lemma below lists the forms the word table recognizes, other than the lemma itself. A form that is not
in the table is unknown and is never analyzed.

### Dictionary Words

The word table knows 365,502 spellings (lemmas and inflected forms) of 223,951 entries, and its sense catalog lists
129,427 senses in 56 curated groups. Besides the lemmas listed below, every other word of the table is a dictionary
word: it has no trained classifier, a word with one part of speech is answered directly with confidence 1, and a word
with several parts of speech returns them as candidates, most frequent first (the encoder models answer it with the
first one; the basic model chooses by tagger and context). A capitalized word is lower-cased before it is looked up.

The lemmas listed below are the 20 trained lemmas (the lemmas that have anchor sentences), with 299 senses (6 of them
project senses) and 56 groups.

## Supported Lemmas

The library supports 20 lemmas with 299 senses in total, listed alphabetically. Each lemma lists its parts of speech and
the forms it recognizes. Under it, every sense gives its id and part of speech, its group, its Open English WordNet
sense key (a project sense has none), its respelling when it has one and its gloss, in inventory order (the most
frequent sense of a part of speech first).
